content:
Several participants have asked how I keep improving my Kaggriculture agents.

First, the unglamorous answer: Codex Sol Ultra is genuinely very good. I say this half-jokingly, but only half. In Kaggriculture, one inventory bug, seat mismatch, illegal queue, or slipped worker action can destroy an otherwise strong strategy. Meticulous engineering is part of strategic strength.

However, I never trust an AI when it calls its own solution “optimal.” My loop is:

Real losses
→ identify one failure mechanism
→ build challengers
→ test multiple teams and both seats
→ reject most candidates
→ freeze the winner
→ test on later episodes

I also retain representative strategies from earlier stages. Optimizing only against the latest Top-30 can lose to older meta generations still active on the leaderboard.

The better prompt is not:

Build the optimal agent.

but:

Where does this agent lose, and what experiment could disprove the proposed improvement?

Why I publish

I publish because I want the community to produce ideas that go beyond meta exploitation.

Currently, copying a strong public meta Notebook can be enough to rise quickly. But that edge is soon absorbed into the next meta, so nothing is fundamentally solved.

I hope this frustration becomes motivation to build genuinely closed-loop agents that discover something beyond another fixed best response.

I have one weaker, more speculative hypothesis: repeated best responses may eventually reach a stable attractor—the “One Piece” of the high-dimensional policy space, or the true final meta. If that happens, rating and matchmaking may favor whoever reached the top earlier, creating some path dependence.

I do not strongly believe this explanation, because it can change with the host’s matchmaking and episode-generation settings.

My main belief is simpler:

The submitted agent may be open-loop, but the research process must be closed-loop.

Latest example:

25/27 Strict-Future | v27 Midgame Meta Reset

Thanks a lot for this. I got in top 10 just because of your notebook but i dont feel good about it bcz its not my work. I'll try your approach and try building better agents and most importantly "my Agents" instead of cloning the next public notebook.

Your openness is appreciated. I can't speak for everyone, but i'm working 2 lanes (and I suspect a lot of others are as well): the first lane clones and then optimizes the current meta, while the second lane builds toward developing new metas. I haven't had any luck developing something new (I genuinely don't know how some people are doing it), but I think I get a little closer every day.

Thank you — I really like the two-lane framing. I may see the boundary between them a little differently, though.

To me, countering the current meta can itself be the process of creating a new meta. If the counter only exploits one specific route, it is probably just a temporary anti-meta. But if it identifies why the current meta works and develops a general response that forces others to adapt, then that response may become the next meta.

So perhaps the real distinction is not optimization versus innovation, but countering a specific implementation versus replacing the principle behind it. In that sense, I think the two lanes are closely connected.

And I completely relate to the difficulty of discovering something genuinely new. Even when an experiment fails, it still feels like one more step toward understanding the game.

Thank you for sharing this important project. When I first tried to participate, I couldn't understand everything because my study approach was a bit outdated, which was somewhat frustrating. ​When I went back and tried again, I realized where the issues were. That’s why I decided to study more deeply. I agree with you that copying or relying on notebook notes in a competition is great at the beginning, but over time, it won't get you to high ranks or help you win prizes simply because everyone has access to the exact same setup. ​The real question is how to evolve, carve your own path, and stand out. I'm not against using starter notebooks, but you need an edge to reach top-tier levels. I remember in one of the competitions, there was a specific approach I unfortunately discovered too late. If only I had asked myself back then, 'Why are people using this specific method?' when I was reading books. ​Ultimately, learning while sharing building AI applications is a wonderful journey. I'm currently learning it through the book Building Ai Agents for Applications. Thank you again
